analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from using job applicants' credit reports in most hiring and employment decisions.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2021 with no cosponsors, was sent to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to stop credit reporting agencies from selling a person's credit report to an employer for hiring, firing, or other employment decisions, except when a law or regulation requires the check or when it is part of a national security investigation. The bill's findings cite research showing credit history does not predict job performance, that job loss and medical bills can sink a credit score, and that credit checks disproportionately screen out Black and Latino applicants and the long-term unemployed. It also bans employers from getting around the rule by asking applicants to hand over the information themselves, and directs the consumer financial protection bureau to write implementing rules within two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Job seekers and workers with damaged credit — people who lost a job, fell behind on bills after a medical crisis or divorce, or were hit by the 2008 financial crisis. The bill's findings note credit checks grew from about 25% of employers in 1998 to 60% by 2011, that poor credit tracks with unemployment and medical debt, and that Black and Latino households on average have lower credit scores, so the ban would remove a screening practice that has little proven link to job performance and weighs hardest on people already struggling.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits credit reporting agencies from furnishing consumer reports bearing on creditworthiness for employment purposes, unless required by federal, state, or local law or regulation or for a national security investigation [S2][S3].

Bars circumvention: an employer who cannot use the report may not directly or indirectly require, request, or pressure an employee or applicant to submit the information as a condition of employment, and applicants cannot waive the protection [S3].

Breaks what the bill's findings call a catch-22 — losing a job damages credit, and damaged credit then blocks getting a new job — and cites research finding no benefit from using credit history to predict job performance or turnover [S3].

Addresses disparate impact: the bill's findings cite studies showing African-American and Latino households on average have lower credit scores, so credit checks may disproportionately screen otherwise qualified minority applicants out of jobs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies and the background screening industry lose the market for employment credit checks. Some employers lose a screening tool they used mainly to reduce theft and embezzlement risk and liability for negligent hiring, per a 2012 HR survey cited in the findings [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and background check firms

drawbacks.text: Employers cited in the bill's own findings said they used credit checks primarily to reduce or prevent theft and embezzlement and to minimize legal liability for negligent hiring; the bill removes that tool for positions handling money unless a law specifically requires a check [S3].

The ban reaches nearly all employment uses, including for promotions and reassignments, not just hiring for sensitive financial positions, which is broader than the roughly ten states that had already restricted employment credit checks at the time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a screening practice that its own documented findings say does not predict job performance and falls hardest on people whose credit was damaged by unemployment, medical bills, or the financial crisis. The cost falls mainly on credit bureaus and screening firms that sell employment reports, and on employers who lose one screening tool; the employer exemption for checks required by law and the national security carve-out limit the downside. The main honest objection is that some employers want credit checks for positions of financial trust, and the bill does not carve those out beyond what existing law requires.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and with zero cosponsors it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Lawson of Florida introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action; the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 without ever leaving committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies and the employment background screening industry, which keep selling credit reports to employers; employers also keep the option of using credit checks in hiring.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus and background screening firms

for.name: Rep. Al Lawson, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and issued no other recorded action; no colleagues cosponsored it.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 24, 2021 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of support was never tested.

industries.industry: Consumer reporting agencies (credit bureaus) and employment background screening firms
industries.note: Employment credit checks are a revenue line for credit bureaus and screening firms; the bill removes most of that market. Their interest in keeping the checks runs against applicants with damaged credit, whom the checks can screen out of jobs.

industries.industry: Employers, especially those screening for positions handling money
industries.note: Employers lose a screening tool they said they used to reduce theft and embezzlement risk and negligent-hiring liability, though the bill's cited research found credit history does not predict job performance. The bill leaves checks available where law or regulation requires them.

industries.industry: Staffing and human resources screening services
industries.note: Firms that run employment verification and screening packages sell credit-based reports to the roughly 60% of employers the bill says used them by 2011; the ban shrinks that service offering.
